intro: Hi! You already know should, have to, must, and the big difference between mustn't and don't have to. Today you go further: when to choose must or have to, how to talk about rules in the past and future (had to, will have to), how to say what you're allowed to do, and how to say something is possible with may, might and could. Warm-up: how do you say 'kemarin saya harus lembur' in English?
teachingNotes: Recap in one line, don't re-teach: from a2-modals-obligation the learner knows should (advice), have to / has to and must (harus), mustn't (dilarang) vs don't have to (tidak perlu), and Do I have to ...?. Stress the node's common errors and say why: *'Yesterday I must work late' -> 'Yesterday I had to work late' (must has no past form; had to is the past of both must and have to). *'We are not allow to smoke here' -> 'We are not allowed to smoke here' (allowed always ends in -ed; learners drop it because the d is hard to hear: allowed sounds like 'a-LAUD', like loud). *'You mustn't come if you're busy' -> 'You don't have to come if you're busy' (mustn't = dilarang; tidak harus / tidak usah = don't have to).

must vs have to: keep it simple. must = the speaker's own feeling that something is important (I must call my grandmother) or a written rule: signs, notices, laws (Visitors must sign in). have to = the obligation comes from outside: a boss, a company, a school, a timetable, a situation (I have to wear a uniform at work. The KRL is broken, so I have to take an ojek). In many sentences both are correct and native speakers mix them, so only test clear cases: who decided (the speaker vs someone else), or turning a sign into a sentence with must. Never mark have to wrong in a sign sentence or must wrong in a 'my boss says' sentence: say which one is more typical and why. Questions still use Do I have to ...? (Must I ...? sounds old-fashioned).

had to / will have to: had to + base verb for every subject (no 'hads to', no 'had to went'); didn't have to = tidak perlu in the past (not 'didn't had to'); Did you have to ...?. Future: will have to / 'll have to / won't have to; *'I will must' is wrong because must has no future form. Accept 'going to have to' as a natural alternative. Indonesian has no tense (Kemarin saya harus lembur / Besok saya harus lembur), so learners keep must or have to: point to the time words (yesterday, last week, tomorrow, next month).

be allowed to: am / is / are allowed to + base verb (present), was / were allowed to (past), will be allowed to (future) = diizinkan / boleh; not allowed to = tidak boleh / dilarang. Questions: Are we allowed to ...?. Indonesian trap: 'Kami tidak diizinkan merokok' has no to be, so learners say 'We not allowed'. Memory aid: allowed is like di-izinkan (di- in Indonesian, -ed in English); teach it as a fixed phrase, NOT as the passive. can / can't for permission are fine in speaking; mustn't and not allowed to both mean forbidden (mustn't sounds like the speaker's or a written rule, not allowed to like rules made by others).

may / might / could + base verb = mungkin (possible, not sure), about now or the future. might is the most common in speaking, may is a bit more formal, could = it's possible. Negative: might not / may not = mungkin tidak (don't use couldn't for this: couldn't means tidak bisa or tidak mungkin). Traps: mungkin is also maybe, a separate word at the start (Maybe I'll come), so *'I maybe come' -> 'I might come' or 'Maybe I'll come'; *'She might at the office' -> 'She might be at the office' (be is needed; Indonesian 'Dia mungkin masih di kantor' has no be); *'It might to rain' / *'It mights rain' (helper word: no to, no -s). Always name the other jobs so nothing looks like a broken rule: could for past ability (When I was five, I could swim) and polite requests (Could you ...? / Could I ...?) from a2-can-could, May I ...? for permission. Same word, different job: the context tells you.

Limits: no must / can't for guessing (He must be tired), no may have / might have / could have + past form, no have got to, needn't, ought to, no passive (allowed is a fixed phrase), no reported speech. If a learner asks, say these come in later lessons. B1 contexts: office and tech (VPN, laptop, server, deadline), KRL, ojek online, campus, hospital, Jakarta and Bandung.

keyPoints.title: must or have to: who makes the rule?
keyPoints.explanation: Both mean harus and are often both correct. A simple guide: must = you feel it's important yourself, or it's a written rule (signs, notices, laws). have to = the rule comes from outside: your boss, your company, a timetable, the situation. In negatives they're still very different: mustn't = dilarang, don't have to = tidak perlu.

examples.en: I must call my grandmother this weekend.
examples.id: Saya harus menelepon nenek akhir pekan ini. (perasaan saya sendiri)

examples.en: Visitors must sign in at reception.
examples.id: Tamu wajib mengisi daftar hadir di resepsionis. (aturan tertulis)

examples.en: I have to use the VPN at home. It's a company rule.
examples.id: Saya harus pakai VPN di rumah. Itu aturan kantor.

id.title: must atau have to: siapa yang membuat aturannya?
id.explanation: Keduanya berarti harus dan sering sama-sama benar. Panduan sederhana: must = kamu sendiri merasa itu penting, atau itu aturan tertulis (papan tanda, pengumuman, undang-undang). have to = aturannya datang dari luar: bosmu, kantormu, jadwal, atau keadaan. Dalam kalimat negatif keduanya tetap sangat berbeda: mustn't = dilarang, don't have to = tidak perlu.

keyPoints.title: had to (past) and will have to (future)
keyPoints.explanation: must has no past and no future form, so English uses have to: had to + base verb for the past (the same for every subject), will have to + base verb for the future. Negatives: didn't have to (tidak perlu, past), won't have to (tidak perlu, future). Questions: Did you have to ...? / Will we have to ...?

examples.en: Yesterday I had to work late.
The meeting was online, so we didn't have to go to the office.
examples.id: Rapatnya online, jadi kami tidak perlu ke kantor.

examples.en: Next year you'll have to pay for the app.
examples.id: Tahun depan kamu harus bayar untuk aplikasinya.

id.title: had to (lampau) dan will have to (masa depan)
id.explanation: must tidak punya bentuk lampau atau masa depan, jadi bahasa Inggris memakai have to: had to + kata kerja dasar untuk masa lalu (sama untuk semua subjek), will have to + kata kerja dasar untuk masa depan. Negatif: didn't have to (tidak perlu, lampau), won't have to (tidak perlu, masa depan). Pertanyaan: Did you have to ...? / Will we have to ...?

keyPoints.title: be allowed to (permission)
keyPoints.explanation: am / is / are allowed to + base verb = boleh, diizinkan. not allowed to = tidak boleh, dilarang. Past: was / were allowed to. You need the to be (am / is / are) and allowed always ends in -ed: say 'We aren't allowed to smoke', not 'We not allow to smoke'.

examples.en: We're allowed to work from home on Fridays.
examples.id: Kami boleh kerja dari rumah setiap Jumat.

examples.en: Students aren't allowed to use phones in the exam room.
examples.id: Mahasiswa tidak boleh memakai HP di ruang ujian.

examples.en: Are we allowed to park here?
examples.id: Apakah kita boleh parkir di sini?

id.title: be allowed to (izin)
id.explanation: am / is / are allowed to + kata kerja dasar = boleh, diizinkan. not allowed to = tidak boleh, dilarang. Lampau: was / were allowed to. Kamu perlu to be (am / is / are), dan allowed selalu berakhiran -ed: katakan 'We aren't allowed to smoke', bukan 'We not allow to smoke'.

keyPoints.title: may, might and could for possibility (mungkin)
keyPoints.explanation: may / might / could + base verb = mungkin: it's possible, but you're not sure. might is the most common in speaking. Negative: might not / may not (mungkin tidak). They are helper words: no to, no -s. Don't confuse them with maybe, a separate word at the start of a sentence: 'Maybe I'll come' or 'I might come', not 'I maybe come'. could also has other jobs you know (I could swim when I was five, Could you help me?): the context tells you which one.

examples.en: Take an umbrella. It might rain later.
The server may be down. Let me check.
examples.id: Servernya mungkin mati. Saya cek dulu.

examples.en: I might not come to the party. I'm very tired.
examples.id: Saya mungkin tidak datang ke pesta. Saya capek sekali.

id.title: may, might dan could untuk kemungkinan (mungkin)
id.explanation: may / might / could + kata kerja dasar = mungkin: bisa terjadi, tapi kamu tidak yakin. might paling sering dipakai saat bicara. Negatif: might not / may not (mungkin tidak). Semuanya kata bantu: tanpa to, tanpa -s. Jangan tertukar dengan maybe, kata terpisah di awal kalimat: 'Maybe I'll come' atau 'I might come', bukan 'I maybe come'. could juga punya tugas lain yang sudah kamu kenal (I could swim when I was five, Could you help me?): konteksnya yang menunjukkan tugas mana.

assessment.prompt:
Sari says: 'I have to wear a uniform at work.' Who decided this? Answer A or B.

B: someone else (it's her company's rule)

someone else
her company
her company's rule
the company
b someone else
assessment.rubric: Correct: B (have to = the obligation comes from outside: her company). A = 0 (that would be must: the speaker's own feeling).

assessment.prompt: A notice at a hospital says: ALL VISITORS: WASH YOUR HANDS BEFORE ENTERING. Write the rule as one sentence with must, starting with 'Visitors'.
acceptableAnswers: visitors must wash their hands before entering
visitors must wash their hands before they enter
visitors must wash their hands
visitors must wash their hands before entering the ward
visitors must wash hands before entering
assessment.rubric: Correct: Visitors must wash their hands (before entering). 'Visitors have to wash their hands' = 70 (correct English, but the item asks for must, the usual word for a written rule). 'must to wash' or 'must washes' = 40. 'mustn't wash' = 0.

acceptableAnswers: last night i had to finish a report for my boss
i had to finish a report for my boss last night
assessment.rubric: Correct: had to finish (must has no past form; had to is the past of must and have to). 'had to finished' = 50 (the verb after had to stays in the base form). 'have to' or 'must' = 0.

acceptableAnswers: pak hasan might be in a meeting now
pak hasan might be in a meeting
he might be in a meeting now
assessment.rubric: Correct: Pak Hasan might be in a meeting (now). 'might is' or 'might in a meeting' = 40 (after might the verb is the base form be). 'mights be' = 50. 'may be' (two words) = 90 (correct English, but the item asks for might).

material.title: must or have to? Who makes the rule

blocks.text:
**Quick recap (A2):** *should* = advice (sebaiknya). *have to / has to* and *must* = necessary (harus). *mustn't* = not allowed (dilarang). *don't have to* = not necessary (tidak perlu).

Now a new question: when both mean *harus*, which one do you choose? In Indonesian there's only one word, *harus*, so this is new for you. A simple guide:
- **must** = **you yourself** feel it's important, or it's a **written rule**: signs, notices, laws.
- **have to** = the rule comes **from outside**: your boss, your company, your school, a timetable, or the situation.

id.text:
**Ulasan singkat (A2):** *should* = saran (sebaiknya). *have to / has to* dan *must* = perlu (harus). *mustn't* = tidak diizinkan (dilarang). *don't have to* = tidak perlu.

Sekarang pertanyaan baru: kalau keduanya berarti *harus*, mana yang dipilih? Bahasa Indonesia hanya punya satu kata, *harus*, jadi ini hal baru untukmu. Panduan sederhana:
- **must** = **kamu sendiri** merasa itu penting, atau itu **aturan tertulis**: papan tanda, pengumuman, undang-undang.
- **have to** = aturannya datang **dari luar**: bosmu, kantormu, sekolahmu, jadwal, atau keadaan.

rows.en: I must call my grandmother this weekend. I miss her.
rows.id: Saya harus menelepon nenek akhir pekan ini. Saya kangen.

rows.en: Visitors must sign in at reception.
rows.id: Tamu wajib mengisi daftar hadir di resepsionis.

rows.en: I have to use the VPN at home. It's a company rule.
rows.id: Saya harus pakai VPN di rumah. Itu aturan kantor.

rows.en: The KRL isn't running, so I have to take an ojek.
rows.id: KRL tidak jalan, jadi saya harus naik ojek.

blocks.text:
**Don't worry about the grey cases.** In many sentences both are correct, and native speakers often mix them: *You must / have to wear a helmet* are both fine. **have to** is the safe choice when you speak. Use the guide only when it's clear who decided.
**British and American:** Americans use *must* less in speaking; they mostly say *have to*.

id.text:
**Jangan pusing dengan kasus abu-abu.** Di banyak kalimat keduanya benar, dan penutur asli sering mencampurnya: *You must / have to wear a helmet* sama-sama benar. **have to** pilihan aman saat bicara. Pakai panduan ini hanya kalau jelas siapa yang memutuskan.
**British dan American:** orang Amerika lebih jarang memakai *must* saat bicara; mereka biasanya bilang *have to*.

blocks.text: **Negatives are still very different.** Your colleague is busy, and you want to say the meeting is optional. 'You mustn't come if you're busy' is wrong: it means coming is **forbidden** (dilarang)! Say **You don't have to come if you're busy** (*tidak usah / tidak harus*). Remember: *tidak harus* = **don't have to**, not mustn't.

id.text: **Bentuk negatif tetap sangat berbeda.** Rekan kerjamu sibuk, dan kamu mau bilang rapatnya tidak wajib. 'You mustn't come if you're busy' itu salah: artinya datang itu **dilarang**! Katakan **You don't have to come if you're busy** (*tidak usah / tidak harus*). Ingat: *tidak harus* = **don't have to**, bukan mustn't.

blocks.prompt: Pak Hasan says: 'I have to be at the bank at 7 every morning.' Why does he use have to?
options: It's a rule from his work.
blocks.explain: have to = the obligation comes from outside: here his job at the bank. must would show his own feeling, and 'not necessary' would be don't have to.

id.prompt: Pak Hasan berkata: 'I have to be at the bank at 7 every morning.' Kenapa dia memakai have to?
id.explain: have to = kewajibannya datang dari luar: di sini dari pekerjaannya di bank. must akan menunjukkan perasaannya sendiri, dan 'tidak perlu' itu don't have to.

id.title: must atau have to? Siapa yang membuat aturannya

material.title: Past and future: had to and will have to

blocks.text:
**must has no past form and no future form.** So when you talk about yesterday or tomorrow, use **have to**:
- Past: **had to** + base verb (*harus* in the past). The same for every subject: *I had to, she had to, they had to*.
- Future: **will have to** (or **'ll have to**) + base verb.

In Indonesian the verb never changes: *Kemarin saya harus lembur*, *Besok saya harus lembur*. In English the time changes the form: look for words like *yesterday, last week, tomorrow, next month*.

id.text:
**must tidak punya bentuk lampau dan masa depan.** Jadi kalau membicarakan kemarin atau besok, pakai **have to**:
- Lampau: **had to** + kata kerja dasar (*harus* di masa lalu). Sama untuk semua subjek: *I had to, she had to, they had to*.
- Masa depan: **will have to** (atau **'ll have to**) + kata kerja dasar.

Dalam bahasa Indonesia kata kerjanya tidak berubah: *Kemarin saya harus lembur*, *Besok saya harus lembur*. Dalam bahasa Inggris, waktu mengubah bentuknya: perhatikan kata seperti *yesterday, last week, tomorrow, next month*.

rows.en: Yesterday I had to work late.
rows.id: Kemarin saya harus lembur.

rows.en: Rina had to take an ojek because the KRL was late.
rows.id: Rina harus naik ojek karena KRL-nya terlambat.

rows.en: The meeting was online, so we didn't have to go to the office.
rows.id: Rapatnya online, jadi kami tidak perlu ke kantor.

rows.en: Next year you'll have to pay for the app.
rows.id: Tahun depan kamu harus bayar untuk aplikasinya.

rows.en: Don't worry. You won't have to work this weekend.
rows.id: Tenang. Kamu tidak perlu kerja akhir pekan ini.

blocks.text:
**The verb after had to stays in the base form.** *had* already shows the past, so: **She had to go**, not 'She had to went'. In negatives and questions use *did* + **have**, like any past simple verb: **I didn't have to pay. Did you have to wait?** (not 'didn't had to').
**Future:** never 'will must'. Say **will have to**.
**Say it:** in fast speech *had to* sounds like 'HAT-ta'.

id.text:
**Kata kerja sesudah had to tetap bentuk dasar.** *had* sudah menunjukkan lampau, jadi: **She had to go**, bukan 'She had to went'. Dalam kalimat negatif dan pertanyaan pakai *did* + **have**, seperti kata kerja past simple lainnya: **I didn't have to pay. Did you have to wait?** (bukan 'didn't had to').
**Masa depan:** jangan 'will must'. Katakan **will have to**.
**Cara mengucapkan:** saat bicara cepat, *had to* terdengar seperti 'HAT-ta'.

blocks.prompt: Yesterday the lift in our office was broken, so I ___ use the stairs.
blocks.explain: Yesterday = past, and must has no past form, so: had to. (lift is British English; Americans say elevator.)

id.prompt: Lengkapi: Yesterday the lift in our office was broken, so I ___ use the stairs.
id.explain: Yesterday = lampau, dan must tidak punya bentuk lampau, jadi: had to. (lift itu British English; orang Amerika bilang elevator.)

id.title: Lampau dan masa depan: had to dan will have to

material.title: be allowed to: boleh and tidak boleh

blocks.text:
To talk about **permission** (izin), use **be allowed to** + base verb:
- **am / is / are allowed to** = *boleh, diizinkan*
- **am / is / are not allowed to** = *tidak boleh, dilarang*
- Past: **was / were (not) allowed to**. Future: **will be allowed to**.
- Question: **Are we allowed to …?** (*Apakah kita boleh …?*)
It's often about rules that other people make: your company, your school, your parents, the building.

id.text:
Untuk membicarakan **izin**, pakai **be allowed to** + kata kerja dasar:
- **am / is / are allowed to** = *boleh, diizinkan*
- **am / is / are not allowed to** = *tidak boleh, dilarang*
- Lampau: **was / were (not) allowed to**. Masa depan: **will be allowed to**.
- Pertanyaan: **Are we allowed to …?** (*Apakah kita boleh …?*)
Biasanya tentang aturan yang dibuat orang lain: kantormu, sekolahmu, orang tuamu, gedungnya.

rows.en: We're allowed to work from home on Fridays.
rows.id: Kami boleh kerja dari rumah setiap Jumat.

rows.en: Students aren't allowed to use phones in the exam room.
rows.id: Mahasiswa tidak boleh memakai HP di ruang ujian.

rows.en: When I was a child, I wasn't allowed to stay up late.
rows.id: Waktu kecil, saya tidak boleh begadang.

rows.en: Are we allowed to bring food into the cinema?
rows.id: Apakah kita boleh bawa makanan ke bioskop?

blocks.text:
**The Indonesian trap: two small parts go missing.** 'We are not allow to smoke here' and 'We not allowed to smoke here' are both wrong. Say **We are not allowed to smoke here.**
- **allowed** always ends in **-ed**. A memory trick: *allowed* is like *di-izinkan*: Indonesian adds *di-*, English adds *-ed*. Learners often drop it because the d is hard to hear: *allowed* sounds like 'a-LAUD' (like *loud*): two syllables, and the -ed adds no extra syllable.
- You need **am / is / are** (or *was / were*), even though Indonesian *Kami tidak diizinkan* has no to be.

id.text:
**Jebakan bahasa Indonesia: dua bagian kecil sering hilang.** 'We are not allow to smoke here' dan 'We not allowed to smoke here' dua-duanya salah. Katakan **We are not allowed to smoke here.**
- **allowed** selalu berakhiran **-ed**. Trik mengingat: *allowed* mirip *di-izinkan*: bahasa Indonesia menambah *di-*, bahasa Inggris menambah *-ed*. Akhiran ini sering hilang karena bunyi d-nya susah terdengar: *allowed* dibaca 'e-LAUD' (seperti *loud*): dua suku kata, dan -ed tidak menambah suku kata.
- Kamu perlu **am / is / are** (atau *was / were*), walaupun *Kami tidak diizinkan* dalam bahasa Indonesia tidak punya to be.

blocks.text: **can, mustn't and allowed.** In everyday speech, *can / can't* also talk about permission: *You can't park here* = *You aren't allowed to park here*. *mustn't* means forbidden too, but it sounds like the speaker's own rule or a written one. **be allowed to** works well for rules made by others, and it has easy past and future forms (*was allowed to, will be allowed to*).

id.text: **can, mustn't dan allowed.** Dalam percakapan sehari-hari, *can / can't* juga dipakai untuk izin: *You can't park here* = *You aren't allowed to park here*. *mustn't* juga berarti dilarang, tapi terdengar seperti aturan dari pembicara sendiri atau aturan tertulis. **be allowed to** cocok untuk aturan yang dibuat orang lain, dan bentuk lampau serta masa depannya mudah (*was allowed to, will be allowed to*).

blocks.prompt: New interns ___ use the company laptop at home.
blocks.explain: be + not + allowed to: aren't allowed to. allowed needs -ed, and the sentence needs are (aren't = are not).

id.prompt: Lengkapi: New interns ___ use the company laptop at home.
id.explain: be + not + allowed to: aren't allowed to. allowed perlu -ed, dan kalimatnya perlu are (aren't = are not).

id.title: be allowed to: boleh dan tidak boleh

blocks.text:
When something is **possible** but you're **not sure**, use **may / might / could** + base verb. In Indonesian: *mungkin*.
- **might** is the most common when you speak.
- **may** is a little more formal (emails, news, work).
- **could** = it's possible.
The negative is **might not / may not** (*mungkin tidak*). These are helper words like *can* and *should*: no *to*, no *-s*.

id.text:
Kalau sesuatu **bisa terjadi** tapi kamu **tidak yakin**, pakai **may / might / could** + kata kerja dasar. Dalam bahasa Indonesia: *mungkin*.
- **might** paling sering dipakai saat bicara.
- **may** sedikit lebih formal (email, berita, kantor).
- **could** = bisa saja terjadi.
Bentuk negatifnya **might not / may not** (*mungkin tidak*). Semuanya kata bantu seperti *can* dan *should*: tanpa *to*, tanpa *-s*.

rows.en: Take an umbrella. It might rain later.
rows.id: Bawa payung. Nanti mungkin hujan.

rows.en: The server may be down. Let me check.
rows.id: Servernya mungkin mati. Saya cek dulu.

rows.en: Don't buy the ticket yet. The price could go down.
rows.id: Jangan beli tiketnya dulu. Harganya bisa saja turun.

rows.en: I might not come to the party. I'm very tired.
rows.id: Saya mungkin tidak datang ke pesta. Saya capek sekali.

blocks.text:
**The Indonesian trap: mungkin = maybe OR might.** *maybe* is a separate word; it usually goes **at the start**: **Maybe I'll come.** *might* goes **before the verb**: **I might come.** Not 'I maybe come'.
And don't forget **be**: *Dia mungkin masih di kantor* → **She might be at the office**, not 'She might at the office'. Indonesian has no to be here, English needs it.

id.text:
**Jebakan bahasa Indonesia: mungkin = maybe ATAU might.** *maybe* adalah kata terpisah; biasanya di **awal kalimat**: **Maybe I'll come.** *might* diletakkan **sebelum kata kerja**: **I might come.** Bukan 'I maybe come'.
Dan jangan lupa **be**: *Dia mungkin masih di kantor* → **She might be at the office**, bukan 'She might at the office'. Bahasa Indonesia tidak memakai to be di sini, bahasa Inggris memerlukannya.

blocks.prompt: The traffic in Jakarta is terrible today. Which sentence is correct?
blocks.explain: might + base verb: might arrive (no to). maybe is a separate word at the start: Maybe we'll arrive late.

id.prompt: Lalu lintas di Jakarta parah sekali hari ini. Kalimat mana yang benar?
id.explain: might + kata kerja dasar: might arrive (tanpa to). maybe adalah kata terpisah di awal kalimat: Maybe we'll arrive late.

material.title: could and may: same word, different job

blocks.text:
Wait: you learnt *could* and *may* before, with a different meaning! Is the rule broken? No. Some helper words have **more than one job**, and the **context** tells you which one.
- **could** (A2): the past of *can* (*When I was five, I could swim* = dulu bisa) and polite requests (*Could you help me?*).
- **could** (new): possibility (*It could rain* = mungkin).
- **May I …?** (A2): asking permission (*bolehkah saya*).
- **may** (new): possibility (*Budi may be late* = mungkin).

id.text:
Tunggu: kamu sudah belajar *could* dan *may* sebelumnya, dengan arti lain! Apakah aturannya rusak? Tidak. Beberapa kata bantu punya **lebih dari satu tugas**, dan **konteks** yang menunjukkan tugas mana.
- **could** (A2): bentuk lampau *can* (*When I was five, I could swim* = dulu bisa) dan permintaan sopan (*Could you help me?*).
- **could** (baru): kemungkinan (*It could rain* = mungkin).
- **May I …?** (A2): minta izin (*bolehkah saya*).
- **may** (baru): kemungkinan (*Budi may be late* = mungkin).

rows.en: When I was young, I could run 5 km.
rows.id: Waktu muda, saya bisa lari 5 km.
rows.note: past ability: a past time + could

id.note: kemampuan di masa lalu: ada waktu lampau + could

rows.en: Could you send me the file, please?
rows.id: Bisa tolong kirim filenya ke saya?
rows.note: a polite request: a question to someone

rows.en: Check the address again. The map could be wrong.
rows.id: Cek alamatnya lagi. Petanya bisa saja salah.
rows.note: possibility: not sure, now or later

id.note: kemungkinan: tidak yakin, sekarang atau nanti

rows.en: May I use your charger?
rows.id: Bolehkah saya pakai charger-mu?

rows.en: The shop may be closed on Sunday.
rows.id: Tokonya mungkin tutup hari Minggu.

blocks.text:
**How to tell:** ask yourself three questions.
1. Is it a question to someone (*Could you …? May I …?*)? → a **request or permission**.
2. Is there a past time (*when I was a child, last year*) and is it about what someone was able to do? → **past ability** (*bisa*, dulu).
3. Is it about now or the future, and you aren't sure? → **possibility** (*mungkin*).

id.text:
**Cara membedakannya:** tanyakan tiga hal.
1. Apakah ini pertanyaan ke seseorang (*Could you …? May I …?*)? → **permintaan atau izin**.
2. Ada waktu lampau (*when I was a child, last year*) dan isinya tentang apa yang dulu bisa dilakukan? → **kemampuan di masa lalu** (*bisa*, dulu).
3. Tentang sekarang atau nanti, dan kamu tidak yakin? → **kemungkinan** (*mungkin*).

blocks.prompt: Which sentence uses may for possibility (mungkin)?
options: Dimas may be at the gym now.
blocks.explain: Dimas may be at the gym = maybe he's at the gym, you aren't sure: possibility. May I …? is a question asking for permission.

id.prompt: Kalimat mana yang memakai may untuk kemungkinan (mungkin)?
id.explain: Dimas may be at the gym = mungkin dia di gym, kamu tidak yakin: kemungkinan. May I …? adalah pertanyaan untuk minta izin.

id.intro: Hai! Kamu sudah kenal should, have to, must, dan beda besar antara mustn't dan don't have to. Hari ini kita melangkah lebih jauh: kapan memilih must atau have to, cara membicarakan aturan di masa lalu dan masa depan (had to, will have to), cara mengatakan apa yang boleh kamu lakukan, dan cara mengatakan sesuatu mungkin terjadi dengan may, might dan could. Pemanasan: apa bahasa Inggrisnya 'kemarin saya harus lembur'?
suggestedQuestions: Apakah salah kalau saya bilang 'You have to wear a helmet', bukan 'You must wear a helmet'?
Kenapa saya tidak boleh bilang 'Yesterday I must work late'?
Bagaimana saya tahu could artinya 'bisa' atau 'mungkin'?

assessment.moa-1:
Sari berkata: 'I have to wear a uniform at work.' Siapa yang memutuskan ini? Jawab A atau B.
A: Sari sendiri (perasaannya sendiri)
B: orang lain (aturan kantornya)
assessment.moa-2: Pengumuman di rumah sakit bertuliskan: ALL VISITORS: WASH YOUR HANDS BEFORE ENTERING. Tulis aturannya sebagai satu kalimat bahasa Inggris dengan must, dimulai dengan 'Visitors'.
assessment.moa-3: Perbaiki kesalahannya: Last night I must finish a report for my boss.
assessment.moa-4: Printer kantor rusak, dan teknisinya baru bisa datang minggu depan. Lengkapi dengan bentuk masa depan dari have to: We ___ print the documents at a copy shop.
assessment.moa-5: Papan di KRL bertuliskan: NO EATING OR DRINKING. Lengkapi dengan allowed: Passengers ___ eat or drink on the train.
assessment.moa-6: Perbaiki kesalahannya: I maybe go to Bandung this weekend.
assessment.moa-7: Tulis ulang dengan might: Maybe Pak Hasan is in a meeting now.
